entities.summary:
Oppian, also known as Oppian of Anazarbus, of Corycus, or of Cilicia, was a 2nd-century Greco-Roman poet during the reign of the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Commodus, who composed the Halieutica, a five-book didactic epic on fishing.

Born in the late 1st century AD, Oppian was a prominent figure in the literary circles of the Eastern Mediterranean, where he drew upon his experiences as a fisherman to craft a unique blend of poetry and practical advice.

Despite his significance as a poet, Oppian's work was largely forgotten until the 19th century, when it was rediscovered by scholars and reevaluated in the context of ancient Greek literature.

Oppian's legacy can be seen in the enduring popularity of his Halieutica, which remains a valuable resource for scholars of ancient fishing practices and the cultural significance of seafood in the Roman Empire.

The Halieutica's detailed descriptions of various fish and seafood dishes have been praised for their vividness and accuracy, providing a unique window into the culinary world of the ancient Mediterranean.

Oppian's influence can also be seen in the development of Western literature, where his emphasis on the importance of practical knowledge and the value of the everyday experience has inspired countless writers and poets throughout history.
